extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of corporate public relations / corporate communications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for public relations practice in corporate organizations, covering research and evaluation, organizational roles, corporate social responsibility, crisis response, codes of conduct, and global communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative versus summative research
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes 'formative' research and 'summative' research with respect to their roles in program evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formative research is used during program development/implementation to shape and improve program activities; summative research measures overall program impact and outcomes after implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research questions by program phase (preparation, implementation, impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify research questions appropriate to the preparation, implementation, and impact phases of public relations programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use phase-appropriate questions to guide data collection and evaluation (e.g., readiness and objectives in preparation; fidelity and reach during implementation; behavior change and reputational impact at impact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outputs versus outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarifies the difference between 'outputs' and 'outcomes' when evaluating PR programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outputs are immediate, tangible products or activities (e.g., press releases, events, media placements); outcomes are changes in awareness, attitudes, behaviors, reputation, or other longer-term effects resulting from outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended steps for conducting evaluation research
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow a set of recommended steps when planning and conducting PR evaluation research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the chapter asks readers to 'List and describe briefly the recommended steps for conducting evaluation research,' typical steps include defining objectives, selecting indicators, choosing methods, collecting data, analyzing results, and reporting findings for program improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major criteria for evaluating preparation, implementation, and impact phases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use distinct evaluative criteria for each phase of a PR program (preparation, implementation, impact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparation criteria might include clarity of objectives and stakeholder analysis; implementation criteria might include message delivery, reach, and fidelity; impact criteria include outcome measures such as changes in stakeholder attitudes, behavior, and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common research methods for evaluating PR programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Be familiar with commonly used research methods for evaluating public relations programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists additional sources on research methods; commonly used methods include surveys, content analysis, media monitoring, focus groups, interviews, and social media analytics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to describe how corporate public relations differs from other sectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate or demonstrate understanding of how corporate public relations practice differs from PR in other sectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate PR often involves a broader array of stakeholders, integration of multiple functions across the organization, and greater emphasis on reputation management, corporate policies, and business outcomes compared with other sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing the impact of social media on corporate reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Outline and evaluate the importance and changing effect of social media on corporate reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that social media: (a) can dictate priorities via citizen journalists and large online audiences; (b) enables direct mass communication; (c) increases speed and scope of attacks (e.g., Facebook takeovers, coordinated postings); and (d) requires familiarity with analytics tools and crisis preparedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of public relations in corporate social responsibility (CSR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe and assess the importance of CSR programs to business and the role public relations plays in creating, implementing, and communicating those programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR executives act as stewards of reputation, align public expectations with business activities, help develop CSR strategy, engage stakeholders, and communicate CSR outcomes; CSR is a major driver of corporate reputation—often second only to product/service quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for designing CSR/sustainability programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements and focal areas companies should target when developing CSR or sustainability programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from SC Johnson show four targeted areas: improving products (eco-friendly ingredients), reducing resource use (energy/emissions), strengthening communities (social progress and public health), and protecting families (preventing insect-borne diseases). Good CSR programs involve measurable impact, stakeholder partnerships, third‑party collaboration, and long-term benefits for communities and supply chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrics for evaluating large-scale/global PR campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative and qualitative metrics to measure the effectiveness of global campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dow/GolinHarris example metrics include postevent research (percent change among key influencers), number of NGOs engaged, media placements count, total impressions, social media metrics (tweets, Facebook impressions), and employee engagement participation rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational placement/reporting structure as an evaluative criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporting relationship of senior PR executives (e.g., reporting to CEO) is a criterion influencing PR effectiveness and corporate reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter cites research correlating CEOs reporting structures with reputation rankings (e.g., higher percentage of CCOs reporting to CEOs in 'Most Admired' companies). Organizational placement affects access, influence, and strategic integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity as a criterion for restoring and maintaining public trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Authenticity—'words and deeds' aligned—is a primary characteristic consumers expect from corporations and a key means to regain public trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites the Arthur Page Society and research showing authenticity is 'the coin of the realm' for reputation; PR practitioners should prioritize genuine behavior, transparency, and consistent messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of an effective Code of Business Conduct (UPS example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key content and structure items that a corporate Code of Business Conduct should include.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UPS Code elements listed: (1) brief intro paragraph; (2) reason for the code and relation to other policies; (3) CEO message including warning against violations; (4) corporate values and management philosophies; (5) Checklist for Leading with Integrity (questions employees should consider); (6) description of program administration; (7) encouragement to raise questions/voice concerns and access to a 24/7 help line; (8) clear anti-retaliation statement; (9) statements on workplace environment, EEO, safety, substance abuse, violence; (10) policies on conflicts of interest, gifts/entertainment, customer relationships, government business, confidential information; (11) antitrust and insider trading policies; (12) intellectual property and trademark protection policies; (13) description of political activities, processes, and contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis communication anti-patterns and preparedness criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Common failures in corporate crisis response and criteria for better crisis management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common failures include slowness to accept responsibility, executives being inaccessible or appearing insincere/uncaring, amplification by third parties, and the 24/7 nature of news via social media. Practitioners should prepare with crisis plans, ensure executive accessibility, use analytics to understand attacks, and have social media familiarity and tools to calibrate responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate visibility to advocacy groups and online vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that corporations are visible targets for advocacy groups and online attacks—the need to evaluate exposure and response capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include orchestrated Facebook takeovers and large-scale hacks (e.g., PlayStation Network). Evaluation should include monitoring, risk assessment, rapid-response protocols, and technical/PR coordination to mitigate reputational and operational damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global communication competency criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Skills and sensitivities required for communicating in a 'borderless world' impacted by globalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should have a global perspective on business and stakeholders, cultural sensitivity, understanding of the global media environment, and the ability to leverage technology to stay connected with colleagues and stakeholders worldwide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using partnerships and third parties in program design and legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The strategic use of partnerships (NGOs, agencies, third-party validators) as a criterion for program credibility and effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SC Johnson, McDonald’s, and Dow examples show that involving third parties (EPA, WWF, NGOs, Live Earth, advisory councils) strengthens program design, implementation, and public credibility; sharing processes with others (e.g., Greenlist) increases industry impact.
